title: The dear friend
hookLine: a friend, not a romantic partner, so the wish stays clean
last: THE BENEFACTOR — THE DOOR IS OPEN.

cards: Who would you text first with good news? Not the person you're supposed to tell. The one you actually want to tell, the friend who'll be happier about it than you are.
That person is today's step. But notice the small rule in today's line: a friend, not a romantic partner. That's not because partners don't matter.
Love for a partner comes tangled with other things: wanting, needing, fear of losing. Today the old manuals ask for someone where the wish can stay clean.

teach.h: METTA COMES FROM MITTA, A FRIEND.
teach.b: Start with the word. The Pali dictionaries derive metta from mitta, which simply means friend. So loving-kindness, at its root, is friendliness.

teach.h: MAY YOU BE WELL, WITH NO HOOK.
teach.b: The feeling you have for a good friend, wanting things to go well for them, with no angle, no deal, is the seed of the whole practice. That's why the dear friend comes early.

In the Visuddhimagga's order, after yourself and a benefactor comes a very dear friend. And the manual adds a caution: with someone very dear, the wish can slide into worry, or even grief if they're suffering.
So you notice that slide, and come back to the simple wish. Not: please don't ever leave. Not: I need you to be okay.

Just: may you be well. The romantic partner is left out at this stage for the same reason. That love is real, and in Buddhist life it's honored, but this stage is about learning a wish with no hook in it.
And the Pali texts take friendship seriously.

teach.h: NOT HALF THE PATH: THE WHOLE.
teach.b: In one conversation, Ananda suggests that good friendship is half of the holy life. The Buddha corrects him: not half. The whole of it, because that's how people grow.
Then comes the practice's quiet trick.
This same wish, the warmth you already have for one friend, is what you'll widen, step by step, to a stranger, a difficult person, everyone.

how: In the traditional order of metta practice, Buddhists extend the wishes to a dear friend after themselves and a benefactor; good friendship, kalyanamittata, is prized in Buddhist teaching.

games.why: he corrects Ananda: good friendship is the whole of the holy life, because that's how people grow on the path.

practice: Bring your friend to mind, their face, their laugh, the way they say your name, and offer the phrases slowly: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease.
If worry creeps in, about their job or their health, notice it and come back to the plain wish. Let it be as simple as friendship is on a good day.

wordCard.voice: Mitta. Friend: the third step of metta, where the wish stays simple and clean.

orig.note: Pali: a friend; metta, loving-kindness, is built from this word.

carryVoice: Your line: friendship, widened. The plain goodwill of one friend is the seed. Day one hundred, done.
